title: Lensfree On-chip Tomographic Microscopy Employing Multi-angle Illumination and Pixel Super-resolution
protocol: Mount the optical fiber on a motorized rotation stage (Thorlabs PRM-1Z8) driven by Thorlabs TDC001 controller to change illumination angle.
Mount the light source, attached to the motorized rotation stage, on a two-dimensional linear X-Y stage (Newport ILS50CC) driven by Newport MFA-PPD controllers for in-plane shifts.
Choose a CMOS sensor array with 5 Mega Pixels and a pixel size of 2.2 μm (IDS Imaging, UI-1485LE-M) as the detector to record wide field-of-view holographic images.
Place samples directly on top of the active area of the detector for imaging.
If implementing dual-axis tomography, mount the detector on a horizontal rotation stage (e.g., Thorlabs RP-01) to rotate the sample and detector in the plane normal to the optic axis.
Using a scalpel or spatula, take a small piece of agar from the Petri dish containing C. elegans culture.
Place the agar piece in a polypropylene vial with 1 ml de-ionized water.
Gently vortex for 0.5-1 min.
Wait for 10-15 min until worms crawl out of the agar into the DI water.
Add 1 ml of 5-10 mM levamisole solution to immobilize the worms.
Wait for 10 min after adding levamisole.
Pipette 5-10 μl of worm sample from the bottom of the vial.
Sandwich the sample between two cover slips.
Adjust the initial angle of the rotation stage to -50°.
Adjust the initial position of the X-Y stage to (0,0).
Set the exposure time of the detector to utilize its dynamic range effectively.
Capture 9 images without changing the angle of the rotation stage.
Move the X-Y stage to a new position in a 3x3 square grid for each image.
Shift each subsequent image by approximately one quarter of a pixel compared to the previous one.
Adjust the initial position of the X-Y stage to (0,0), which is the HOME position.
Increase the angle of the rotation stage by increments of 2° until reaching +50°.
Repeat steps capturing images and moving the X-Y stage for each new angle increment.
Digitally process each set of 9 images using pixel super-resolution algorithms.
Obtain one high-resolution (HR) projection hologram per angle.
Reconstruct 51 projection images from the pixel super-resolved holograms.
Back-project the set of 51 projection images using TomoJ in ImageJ.
Output a three-dimensional image (tomograms) of the sample.
